data.command: Explain T1547 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution

data.text:
# T1547 — Boot or Logon Autostart Execution

**Tactics:** Persistence, Privilege Escalation
**Platforms:** Windows, macOS, Linux

## Overview

T1547 is a MITRE ATT&CK technique where adversaries configure operating system settings to automatically execute a program during system boot or user logon. Because these autostart mechanisms are legitimate OS features, abusing them lets malware survive reboots and re-execute every time a user signs in — often with the privileges of that user, or SYSTEM-level privileges if the mechanism runs before logon.

The core idea: instead of tricking a victim into running the payload again, the attacker registers the payload once and lets the operating system relaunch it indefinitely.

## Common Sub-Techniques

| Sub-technique | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **T1547.001** | Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder — the most common method. Keys like `HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run` and `HKLM\...\CurrentVersion\Run`, or dropping a shortcut into the user's Startup folder |
| **T1547.002** | Authentication Packages — DLLs loaded by LSASS at boot |
| **T1547.003** | Time Providers — DLLs loaded by the Windows Time service |
| **T1547.004** | Winlogon Helper DLL — hijacking `Userinit` or `Shell` values under the Winlogon key |
| **T1547.005** | Security Support Providers (SSPs) — injected into LSASS |
| **T1547.006** | Kernel Modules and Extensions — malicious drivers (Windows) or kexts (macOS) loading at boot |
| **T1547.008** | LSASS Driver — a fake driver registered to load into LSASS |
| **T1547.009** | Shortcut Modification — altering an existing `.lnk` file's target to run malware alongside (or instead of) the legitimate program |
| **T1547.010** | Port Monitors — DLLs loaded by the print spooler (runs as SYSTEM) |
| **T1547.012** | Print Processors — similar spooler-based persistence |
| **T1547.014** | Active Setup — executes per-user payloads before the desktop appears |
| **T1547.015** | Login Items — macOS equivalent (Launch Agents/Daemons are covered under T1543) |

## Why Attackers Like It

- **Low effort, high durability:** One registry write or file drop persists across reboots.
- **Blends in:** Run keys and Startup folders contain legitimate entries (OneDrive, Teams, updaters), so malicious entries can hide in plain sight.
- **Privilege inheritance:** HKLM-based autostarts, print monitors, and LSASS-loaded components execute as SYSTEM, doubling as privilege escalation.
- **No exploit needed:** It abuses intended functionality, so it works on fully patched systems.

## Typical Indicators

- New values under `...\CurrentVersion\Run`, `RunOnce`, `RunServices`, or `Winlogon` keys
- Files appearing in `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup` or the equivalent `ProgramData` path
- Binaries in autostart locations with unsigned executables, random names, or paths in temp/user-writable directories
- Modified `.lnk` files pointing to scripts or unusual interpreters (`powershell.exe`, `rundll32.exe`, `mshta.exe`)

## Detection

- **Sysmon** Event IDs 12/13/14 (registry create/set/rename) and 11 (file create) targeting autostart locations
- **Autoruns** (Sysinternals) or `Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand` for baseline-vs-current comparisons
- EDR rules flagging writes to ASEPs (Auto-Start Extensibility Points) by non-installer processes
- File-integrity monitoring on Startup folders and spooler driver directories

## Mitigation

- Deny standard users write access to HKLM autostart keys and shared Startup folders
- Application allowlisting (AppLocker, WDAC) so unauthorized binaries can't execute even if registered
- Alert on and restrict unsigned driver/SSP/print monitor registration
- Regularly audit autostart entries against a known-good baseline

In short: T1547 is the classic "set it and forget it" persistence technique — simple to execute, easy to overlook, and a staple of commodity malware and APT intrusions alike.
